newsitem.title: USA: U.S. April retail sales slacken, give Fed leeway.
newsitem.headline: U.S. April retail sales slacken, give Fed leeway.

text.p: U.S. retail sales came in as expected in April, leaving the Federal Reserve leeway to pause in further tightening, economists said.

Sales fell 0.3 percent and 0.1 percent excluding autos. The Fed's policy-making arm meets next week and analysts were split as to whether it would vote to ratchet up interest rates by another 25 basis points, as it did at its last meeting.
"If the Fed wants to pause, this gives them some comfort. But there are still plenty of reasons for them to move," said Tim O'Neil, chief economist at the Bank of Montreal.
O'Neil said that even with a slowing in sales in the second quarter, demand remained strong. First quarter sales were strong that a slowdown was inevitable, but the pace remained strong, he said.

"We continue to see an acceleration in wages and disposable personal income," he said. Consumer spending was growing at a more than sustainable rate even given a stronger dollar -- which has been weakening of late, he said.
O'Neil saw the Fed tightening at least twice more based on the strong underlying economy. Even if the dollar continued to weaken, results would not be seen until next year, he said.
Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said the number suggested the economy was weakening.
Platt said he had been expecting a second quarter growth rate of 2.6 percent, but he was now in the process of lowering that forecast to 2.2 percent or 2.3 percent.
"The Fed expected a slowdown and it looks like it's here," said Brian Westbury, chief economist at Griffin, Kubik, Stephens & Thompson Inc.
Consumer spending had grown by 6.4 percent in the first quarter.
Wesbury said the number could relieve a lot concern about potential inflation, but that with a 4.9 percent unemployment rate the Fed would still need to tighten.
He said the Fed's economic models would be flashing warning signals with unemployment at such low levels. However, Wesbury said he believed signs of a slowdown were real.
